subsystems.name: Fusion core
subsystems.role: a compact field-reversed configuration: a plasma torus with closed field lines and no toroidal coils through its centre.

subsystems.name: Superconducting magnets
subsystems.role: generate the steady field that confines and stabilises the plasma.

subsystems.name: Heating and fuelling
subsystems.role: raises the plasma to fusion temperature and feeds it deuterium and helium-3.

subsystems.name: Magnetic nozzle
subsystems.role: shapes the escaping plasma into a directed exhaust, converting thermal energy into thrust.

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: draws electricity from the same reaction for the spacecraft's systems.
parts: turbine and alternator, or direct conversion of charged fusion products

subsystems.name: Shielding and fuel cycle
subsystems.role: protects the vehicle from the neutrons that side reactions still produce, and manages scarce helium-3.

buildSteps.title: Settle the plasma physics
buildSteps.detail: Small experiments such as the Princeton Field-Reversed Configuration must show that an FRC can be formed, sustained and heated by rotating magnetic fields without falling apart.

buildSteps.title: Design the burn
buildSteps.detail: Choose fuel and operating point. Deuterium–helium-3 is favoured because most of its energy leaves as charged particles that a magnetic nozzle can steer, but it needs far higher temperatures than deuterium–tritium and still produces some neutrons.

buildSteps.title: Wind the magnets
buildSteps.detail: High-temperature superconducting coils are wound and potted so they keep their shape under the forces of a high field, then enclosed in a cryostat.

buildSteps.title: Build the core vessel
buildSteps.detail: A vacuum chamber is made with a constricted throat at the exhaust end and fitted with radio-frequency antennas and injectors.

buildSteps.title: Add the nozzle and instrumentation
buildSteps.detail: Expanding coils are mounted downstream of the throat, with probes and a thrust stand to measure what the exhaust actually does in vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Close the power loop
buildSteps.detail: Heat is taken from the machine into a turbine and alternator, and waste heat is rejected through radiators. The electricity partly feeds back into the magnets, heating and controls.

buildSteps.title: Test on the ground, then in orbit
buildSteps.detail: A prototype is run in a large vacuum chamber, measuring thrust, specific impulse and net power over long durations. Only then does a flight demonstration make sense.

prerequisites.why: FRCs have been created and sustained in laboratory devices, but not held in a hot, fusion-burning state.
deuterium–helium-3 fusion needs temperatures well above deuterium–tritium, which itself has not yet produced net power in a magnetic device.
compact, high-field coils are what make a small fusion core conceivable at all.
demonstrated in laboratory plasma thrusters, but never with a fusion-grade exhaust.
helium-3 is extremely scarce on Earth, so the concept assumes extraction from lunar regolith or planetary atmospheres that does not exist.
a fusion drive must reject waste heat and absorb neutrons without carrying tonnes of inert mass.

pathway.milestone: laboratory FRC experiments and paper studies of direct fusion drive missions
pathway.unlocks: a physics basis and plausible mission profiles.

pathway.milestone: a ground prototype that sustains a hot FRC and produces measurable thrust in a vacuum chamber
pathway.unlocks: confidence that one machine can give both power and propulsion.

pathway.milestone: an in-space demonstration of a small drive
pathway.unlocks: real data on reliability, heat rejection and thrust over months.

pathway.milestone: operational drives for outer solar system transport
pathway.unlocks: transit times of months rather than years, and abundant power at the destination — but not Earth launch, since thrust-to-weight is far too low.
